memorial_note: Titanic is the final resting place of about 1,500 people who died on 15 April 1912. Explore with care: observe, photograph and leave the wreck undisturbed.

entries.title: RMS Titanic wreck site
paragraphs: RMS Titanic sank on 15 April 1912 on her maiden voyage after striking an iceberg. About 1,500 people died.

The wreck lies about 3,800 m down in the North Atlantic. A French–American expedition led by Jean-Louis Michel (IFREMER) and Robert Ballard (WHOI) found it on 1 September 1985. Cameras towed from RV Knorr first revealed a boiler; the team followed the debris north to the ship.
The bow and stern rest about 600 m apart and face opposite ways. Hull fragments, machinery and personal belongings are scattered across the surrounding seabed.
GMRT survey cells here span about 45 × 61 m. Magellan's proprietary 2022 photogrammetric scan is not used in this dive.

facts.label: Protection
facts.value: US–UK Agreement in force 18 November 2019; in situ preservation preferred

entries.title: The bow section
paragraphs: The bow stands upright and remains more intact than the stern. Its impact disturbed and ploughed the sediment, leaving marks visible in the 2010 sonar survey.

Iron-eating microbes have been slowly consuming the steel since 1912. They leave rusticles, icicle-like growths of rust that hang from every surface. In 2019 divers in the submersible Limiting Factor found that the starboard officers' quarters, including the captain's cabin and his bathtub, had collapsed. In 2024, RMS Titanic Inc. documented a fallen 4.5 m (15 ft) section of port-side bow railing, confirmed by multibeam imagery.

entries.title: The stern section
paragraphs: The stern lies about 600 m from the bow and is much more badly damaged. WHOI's 2010 images show its collapsed decks and distorted hull. It sank more slowly than the bow.
The stern turned around as it sank, so its rear end now points back towards the bow. The two halves of the ship face in opposite directions.
In 1986, Ballard returned and placed a bronze Titanic Historical Society memorial plaque on the stern to honour those who died.

entries.title: The boiler field
paragraphs: Titanic had 29 coal-fired boilers: 24 double-ended and five single-ended. Each was about 4.8 m (15 ft 9 in) in diameter, according to the 1912 British inquiry. Boilers are among the machinery documented in the wreck's debris field.
One boiler was the first object the 1985 expedition recognised. Early on 1 September, the cameras showed its distinctive rivets; the team followed the debris north to the wreck.

entries.title: The debris field
paragraphs: As the ship broke apart, thousands of objects fell 3.8 km through the dark water: coal, hull plates, furniture, crockery, bottles, and the belongings of passengers and crew. Heavy pieces fell almost straight down. Lighter pieces drifted with the currents and settled in long trails.

The 2010 expedition used two REMUS 6000 autonomous vehicles and an ROV to survey the wreck site. WHOI describes mapping 15–20 square miles (about 39–52 km²) of seafloor. NOAA's account distinguishes the broad scatter from close-up surveys of particular clusters of wreckage.
Pairs of shoes still lie where bodies once came to rest. They are among the most moving sights at the site, and a reminder that this is a grave.
This scan marks the gap between the bow and stern. The survey area extends well beyond the two hull sections.

entries.title: Where the "Big Piece" lay
paragraphs: The "Big Piece", also called "The Chunk", is a recovered section of hull with portholes spanning C-Deck cabins and D-Deck kitchens. RMS Titanic Inc. describes it as a 17-ton section.

Recovery work began in 1994. Weather and equipment problems stopped an attempt in 1996; the section was finally raised in 1998. The expedition operator reports that it was subsequently divided into two sections.
The hull section is no longer on the seabed. This marker lies in the stern-side debris area.

entries.title: The memorial plaque
paragraphs: In 1986, Robert Ballard returned to the wreck and placed a bronze Titanic Historical Society memorial plaque on the stern in honour of those who died.
NOAA treats Titanic as a grave site and maritime memorial. The US–UK agreement entered into force on 18 November 2019 and favours preserving the wreck in place.
This scan marks a memorial site on the stern.

entries.title: An abyssal channel
paragraphs: The wreck rests on a nearly flat stretch of seabed south-east of the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. The ground varies by only a few metres over hundreds of metres. About 5 km to the north-west, the open survey data shows a shallow channel running roughly north-north-east to south-south-west. It is about a kilometre wide and 50–60 m deep.
The survey grid records the channel shape and depth. It does not establish when the channel formed or which currents and sediment flows shaped it.
Unlike the wreck, this feature is real survey data from the GMRT grid (about 45 x 61 m per cell). It has no published name that we could find.

facts.label: Relief
facts.value: about 50–60 m below the surrounding seabed
